questions.q: In blue-green deployment, what state is the green environment in before the cutover?
options: Fully deployed and verified, but receiving 0% of real traffic
Partially deployed, receiving a small percentage of traffic
Not yet deployed at all until the exact moment of cutover
Running on the same instances as blue, sharing traffic evenly
questions.explain: Green is deployed and verified -- health checks, smoke tests -- entirely before it receives a single real request.

questions.q: What actually happens at the moment of a blue-green cutover, per this lesson?
options: A full redeploy of the application to new servers
A routing change at the gateway/load balancer, not a redeploy
Both environments are torn down and rebuilt simultaneously
The model weights are retrained on the new instance
questions.explain: The cutover is just a routing switch -- that's exactly what makes it near-instant in either direction.

questions.q: What is the main cost trade-off of blue-green deployment, according to this lesson?
options: It requires permanently doubling your team's on-call rotation
It only works for stateless applications with no database
It makes rollback impossible once the cutover happens
Both environments run at full capacity during the overlap, doubling compute cost for that period
questions.explain: Blue and green both run at full capacity until blue is torn down -- for GPU-backed inference containers, that's a real cost, not a rounding error.

questions.q: What AI-specific wrinkle does this lesson say blue-green deployment has that a stateless web app doesn't?
options: AI apps cannot use a load balancer at all
Blue and green can behave differently even with identical code, due to things like a different model checkpoint or GPU driver
AI apps can only be deployed using rolling updates, never blue-green
Green environments for AI apps never need a health check
questions.explain: A different pinned model checkpoint, inference library version, or GPU driver can make green behave differently even though the application code is unchanged.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a 200 OK health check isn't sufficient to verify green for an AI app?
options: Because HTTP health checks don't exist for containerized services
Because 200 OK only applies to blue, never to green
Because a green service can be 'up' while silently serving a different model, which a plain health check won't catch
Because health checks are only used during rolling updates, not blue-green
questions.explain: The lesson's point: verifying green needs known test prompts compared against blue's known-good outputs, not just a 200 response, since a silently different model is a worse failure than an outage.
